verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the holy ones who are [in Ephesus] and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
verse.note: The brackets mark words that are missing from the earliest surviving manuscripts of the letter, including the oldest papyrus copy and the original text of the two great fourth-century codices. Many scholars think the letter was first written to circulate among several communities, with the place name added later; others hold that 'in Ephesus' is original. The question remains open.

The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ,
just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, to be holy and blameless before him in love.
verse.note: The phrase stands between two clauses and can go with either. This translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition and takes it with what precedes: 'holy and blameless before him in love'. Many translations instead attach it to the next verse: 'In love he predestined us'. Both readings have strong scholarly support.

verse.text: He predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will,
to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he graced us in the Beloved.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace
which he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight.
He made known to us the secret of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'mystery', which in modern English suggests a puzzle or something that cannot be understood. In the period, and in the Greek version of Daniel, the word meant a secret, especially a divine plan kept hidden until God discloses it. Here the point is precisely that it has now been made known. Most translations keep 'mystery' as an established term.

verse.text: as a plan for the fullness of the times: to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth. In him

note.traditional: to gather together in one; to unite

verse.note: Traditional renderings are 'gather together in one' or 'unite'. The verb was used for summing up an argument or adding items up into one total, and Romans 13:9 uses it for the commandments being 'summed up' in a single saying. Many scholars explain it here as bringing all things together under Christ as head, so 'unite' is a fair paraphrase. 'Sum up' keeps the word's ordinary sense.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here.

verse.text: we were also made his portion, having been predestined according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will,

note.term: we were also made his portion

verse.note: The verb means to assign or be assigned by lot, and occurs only here in the New Testament. It can mean 'we were allotted a share', the traditional 'we obtained an inheritance'. It can also mean 'we were allotted to God as his share', echoing the Old Testament description of Israel as the Lord's portion. This translation takes the second sense, which suits the passive form and the 'possession' of verse 14, but the question is disputed.

verse.text: so that we who first hoped in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the good news of your salvation—in him, when you also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,
who is the down payment on our inheritance, until the redemption of his own possession, to the praise of his glory.
verse.note: Traditional renderings are 'earnest', 'pledge' or 'guarantee'. The word is a commercial term, borrowed from Semitic usage, for the first instalment of a payment that binds the payer to deliver the rest. 'Down payment' conveys that the Spirit is a first part of the inheritance itself, which a bare promise of it would not.

verse.text: For this reason I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the holy ones,
do not stop giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,

note.term: a spirit of wisdom and revelation
note.traditional: the Spirit of wisdom and revelation

verse.note: The Greek has no article and could mean a disposition of wisdom given by God, or the Holy Spirit as the one who gives wisdom and reveals. Many interpreters prefer the second, since revelation is something the Spirit gives and not a human disposition. The lower-case rendering follows the wording without excluding that reading.

verse.text: the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the holy ones,
and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his mighty strength,
which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly realms,
far above every rule and authority and power and lordship, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.

note.term: every rule and authority and power and lordship
note.traditional: all principality, and power, and might, and dominion

verse.note: These four terms were ordinary words for government and rank, but Jewish writings of the period also used such lists for orders of spiritual beings thought to stand behind the visible world. Most scholars think the letter has chiefly these unseen powers in view, as in 3:10 and 6:12. The point is that Christ is enthroned over every one of them, whatever it is called.

verse.text: And he put all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the assembly,

note.term: he put all things under his feet

verse.note: The wording echoes Psalm 8:6, which speaks of God placing all things under the feet of humankind, and is here applied to Christ. The seating 'at his right hand' in verse 20 likewise echoes Psalm 110:1. A reader steeped in the Greek Scriptures would have heard both allusions, though neither is introduced as a quotation.

The traditional rendering is 'church', which now commonly means a building or an institution. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is near-universal in English Bibles and readers know what it refers to. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation to show the word as it was heard.

verse.text: which is his body, the fullness of the one who fills all things in every way.

note.term: who fills all things in every way

verse.note: The verb form can be read as active in sense ('who fills all things') or as passive ('who is being filled'). Most translations take the first, as here, in line with 4:10, where Christ is said to fill all things. On the passive reading, Christ is himself being completely filled, whether by God or by the assembly as his body. The closing phrase, literally 'all in all', may mean 'in every respect' or 'in all things'.

verse.text: And you were dead in your offenses and sins,
in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the domain of the air, of the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.
verse.note: The Greek word means an age or era; older versions paraphrased it as 'course' and several modern ones as 'ways'. The phrase joins two expressions usually found separately, 'this age' and 'this world', to describe the present order of things. A minority of scholars read it as a personal power, 'the Aeon of this world', parallel to the ruler named next; most do not.

The air, the region between the earth and the heavens, was widely thought in antiquity to be the home of spirits. The word traditionally rendered 'power' means authority, and here the sphere in which authority is exercised, hence 'domain'. The ruler is not named, but readers have consistently understood the devil to be meant.

'Spirit' is in the genitive case, so by strict grammar it depends on 'ruler' (the ruler of the spirit) or stands in parallel with 'domain' or 'air'. Most English versions write 'the spirit', identifying it with the ruler himself, which gives a smoother sense but is not what the grammar most naturally says. The translation keeps the genitive; the question is disputed, and on either reading one hostile power is in view.

verse.text: Among them we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, carrying out the wishes of the flesh and of the mind, and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.
But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead in our offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
so that in the coming ages he might display the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—
verse.note: 'This' is neuter in Greek, while 'grace' and 'faith' are both feminine nouns, so it most naturally refers to the whole fact of being saved by grace through faith. That is the majority scholarly view. A long-standing alternative takes 'this' to be faith specifically, making faith itself the gift.

verse.text: not from works, so that no one may boast.
For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them.
Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands—
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations', and in the plural in Jewish usage it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. It is one word in Greek.

note.term: made in the flesh by hands
note.traditional: made in the flesh by hands

verse.note: 'Made by hands' is a pointed word. In the Greek Old Testament it is a regular term for idols, and elsewhere in the New Testament it describes temples and other things of merely human construction. Using it of circumcision presents the labels 'circumcision' and 'uncircumcision' as distinctions at the level of the body.

verse.text: that at that time you were apart from Christ, shut out from citizenship in Israel and foreigners to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall, the hostility, in his flesh,

note.term: the barrier of the dividing wall

verse.note: Literally 'the dividing wall of the fence'. Many readers see an allusion to the stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple beyond which Gentiles were forbidden to go on pain of death, known from Josephus and from surviving warning inscriptions. Others think of the law itself, which Jewish writers of the period could describe as a fence around Israel. The reference is uncertain, and the two ideas are not exclusive.

The Greek syntax across verses 14–15 is disputed. 'The hostility' may explain what the dividing wall is (as here), or it may be the object of 'nullifying' together with the law: 'having nullified in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments'. Likewise 'in his flesh' can go with breaking down the wall or with nullifying the law. The translation keeps the Greek order so that both connections remain possible.

verse.text: nullifying the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that in himself he might create the two into one new person, making peace,
verse.note: The Greek word means a human being, not specifically a male. Some modern versions use 'one new humanity', which is the point, but the image is of a single figure created in Christ out of two groups. 'Person' keeps that image.

verse.text: and might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, killing the hostility by it.
And he came and announced the good news of peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near;
for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
So then, you are no longer foreigners and resident aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household,
verse.note: 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verse.note: The word comes from the Greek version of Isaiah 28:16, where it is a stone laid in a foundation. Most scholars take it here as the cornerstone from which a building's lines are set. Some argue for the capstone or keystone that completes the structure at the top; the evidence for that sense is later and the question remains open.

verse.text: in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord,
verse.note: The best-attested Greek text has no article, which in strict grammar would mean 'every building', as though several structures were growing into one temple. Most scholars and translations read 'the whole building', since Greek of this period uses the form loosely and the context describes a single structure. Some manuscripts add the article, making that sense explicit.

verse.text: in whom you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles—
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'; in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish way of referring to all the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is one Greek word throughout.

note.term: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles—
note.traditional: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,

verse.note: The sentence has no main verb and breaks off. Most interpreters think Paul digresses in verses 2–13 and resumes at verse 14, where 'For this reason' is repeated. A minority supply a verb here: 'I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus.'

verse.text: if indeed you have heard of the administration of God’s grace that was given to me for you:
verse.note: The word means the management of a household or estate, and by extension an arrangement or a task of management. Here it may be the responsibility entrusted to Paul ('stewardship', 'commission') or the way God has arranged for his grace to be dispensed ('plan'). The same word recurs in verse 9, where God's arrangement is more clearly in view; 'administration' is used in both places to keep the link visible.

verse.text: by revelation the secret was made known to me, as I wrote above in brief.
verse.note: In the period, and especially in the Greek version of Daniel, this word means a secret, in particular a purpose of God that is hidden until he discloses it. 'Mystery' now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul's point is that the secret has been revealed and can be stated plainly (verse 6). Most translations keep 'mystery', usually explaining it in this sense.

verse.text: When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the secret of Christ,
which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit:
that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news,
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for good tidings, such as news of a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains common. 'Good news' is used here because it carries the plain sense and keeps the link with the related verb in verse 8, 'to bring … the good news'.

verse.text: of which I became a servant according to the gift of God’s grace, given to me according to the working of his power.
To me, less than the least of all the holy ones, this grace was given: to bring the Gentiles the good news of the unfathomable riches of Christ,
verse.note: The word refers to all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

verse.text: and to enlighten everyone as to what is the administration of the secret hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
so that the richly varied wisdom of God might now be made known through the assembly to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly places,
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation; it should not be heard as a single meeting.

verse.text: in keeping with the purpose of the ages that he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord,
in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

note.traditional: by the faith of him; through faith in him

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'through the faith of him'. The majority reading takes this as faith directed toward Christ. A substantial number of scholars read it as Christ's own faithfulness: 'through his faithfulness'. The grammar allows either.

verse.text: So I ask you not to lose heart at my afflictions on your behalf, which are your glory.

note.term: I ask you not to lose heart
note.traditional: I desire that ye faint not

verse.note: The Greek names neither the person asked nor who might lose heart. Most take it as a request to the readers not to be discouraged by Paul's imprisonment. It could also be a prayer to God that the readers not lose heart or, less probably, that Paul himself not lose heart.

verse.text: For this reason I bend my knees before the Father,
from whom every family in the heavens and on earth takes its name,
verse.note: The Greek word for a family or clan (patria) is formed from the word for father (patēr), so a hearer caught a link with 'the Father' in the previous verse that English cannot reproduce. The word means a group descended from a common ancestor, not 'fatherhood' in the abstract. The older rendering 'the whole family' is unlikely without the article in Greek.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that this translation keeps wherever it occurs. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'.

verse.text: that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, and that you, rooted and grounded in love,
verse.note: In the Greek, 'in love' stands between the clause about Christ dwelling in their hearts and the words 'rooted and grounded', and could belong to either. The edition translated here punctuates it with what precedes: 'that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, in love'. Most translations and commentators attach it to 'rooted and grounded', as here; the punctuation is editorial and not part of the ancient text.

verse.text: may be strong enough to grasp, with all the holy ones, what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled to all the fullness of God.
Now to him who is able to do beyond everything, far more than all we ask or conceive, according to the power at work in us,
to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus, to all the generations of the age of the ages. Amen.

note.term: to all the generations of the age of the ages
note.traditional: throughout all ages, world without end; throughout all generations, for ever and ever

verse.note: The Greek piles up time expressions in a Semitic style: literally 'to all the generations of the age of the ages'. The phrase is an emphatic way of saying 'for all time without end', and most translations paraphrase it so. The literal form is kept here because the letter has spoken repeatedly of 'the ages' (verses 9 and 11).

verse.text: I, then, the prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk in a way worthy of the calling with which you were called,
with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
verse.note: Older translations have “meekness,” which now suggests weakness or timidity. The Greek word describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive, without any implication of weakness. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the mainstream modern rendering.

verse.text: making every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
One body and one Spirit, just as you were also called in the one hope of your calling;
one Lord, one faith, one baptism;
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
Therefore it says: “When he ascended on high, he took captives captive; he gave gifts to people.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 68:18 (67:19 in the Septuagint). Both the Hebrew and the Septuagint say that the victor “received gifts among people,” whereas the wording here says he “gave” them; a similar reading appears in the later Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms, and scholars debate whether the author follows an existing interpretive tradition or adapts the text to his point. The introductory “it says” could also be translated “he says,” with God as the speaker.

verse.text: Now what does “he ascended” mean, if not that he also descended to the lower regions of the earth?

note.term: the lower regions of the earth
note.traditional: the lower parts of the earth

verse.note: The phrase can mean the regions beneath the earth, that is, the realm of the dead, or “the lower regions, namely the earth,” in which case the descent is Christ’s coming into the world. Both readings have strong scholarly support, and a minority takes the descent as the giving of the Spirit after the ascension. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek. Some manuscripts add “first” after “descended.”

verse.text: The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.
And it was he who gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as shepherds and teachers,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a shepherd, used as a picture of those who look after a community. “Pastor” is the Latin word for shepherd but now names a church office, and this is the one place where most translations use it instead of “shepherds.” Because “shepherds and teachers” share a single article in Greek, many scholars think one group, or two closely overlapping groups, is meant.

verse.text: to equip the holy ones for the work of service, for the building up of the body of Christ,
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

note.traditional: for the work of the ministry

verse.note: The three phrases of this verse can be read as parallel, so that the leaders are given for equipping, for ministry and for building up. Here, as in most modern translations, they are read in sequence: the leaders equip all the holy ones, who then do the work of service. The Greek word covers service of many kinds, from waiting at table to carrying out a commission, whereas “ministry” now suggests clergy.

verse.text: until we all come to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full-grown man, to the measure of the stature of Christ’s fullness,
verse.note: The Greek uses the word for an adult male with an adjective meaning complete or fully grown, in contrast to the “infants” of the next verse. The whole community is pictured as a single person growing to adulthood. Older versions have “a perfect man”; many modern ones paraphrase as “maturity” or “mature manhood.”

verse.text: so that we may no longer be infants, tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, through the trickery of people, through cunning that serves the scheming of error,
but rather, speaking the truth in love, may grow up in every way into him who is the head, Christ,
verse.note: The verb can mean telling the truth or, more broadly, being truthful and holding to what is true in conduct as well as speech. Most translations have “speaking the truth,” which fits the contrast with deceitful teaching in the previous verse. Some scholars prefer “living the truth” or “being truthful.”

verse.text: from whom the whole body, joined and held together through every supporting ligament, as each single part does its work in due measure, brings about the body’s growth, so that it builds itself up in love.
So I say this and insist on it in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the futility of their minds,
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” In the plural it is the regular Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples, and this translation renders the one word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense. The readers were themselves of non-Jewish origin (2:11), so the word here points to the way of life of peoples who do not know God.

verse.text: being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts.
They have lost all feeling and have given themselves over to debauchery, for the practice of every kind of impurity, with greed.
But that is not how you learned Christ,
if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, just as truth is in Jesus,
that you are to lay aside the old person who belongs to your former way of life and is being corrupted through the desires that come from deceit,
verse.note: The three infinitives in verses 22–24 (lay aside, be made new, put on) give the content of what the readers were taught. They can be read as instructions still to be carried out, as here, or as statements of what happened at conversion (“that you have laid aside the old person”). The parallel in Colossians 3:9–10 speaks of it as already done. The image is of taking off and putting on clothing.

note.traditional: the old man; the old self

verse.note: The Greek word means a human being, not specifically a male, and not quite “self” in the modern psychological sense. The phrase denotes the person one was before, seen as a whole way of being human. Some scholars take it corporately, of the old humanity as against the new humanity created in Christ (compare 2:15).

verse.text: to be made new in the spirit of your mind,
and to put on the new person, created in God’s likeness in the righteousness and holiness that come from truth.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so “righteousness” here covers doing what is right and just. “Holiness” translates a word different from the usual one for “holy”; it denotes devotion to God, and the pair was a common Greek way of summing up right conduct toward people and toward God. “That come from truth” answers “that come from deceit” in verse 22; many translations instead render “true righteousness and holiness.”

verse.text: Therefore, laying aside falsehood, speak the truth, each of you with your neighbor, because we are members of one another.
Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,

note.term: Be angry and do not sin
note.traditional: Be ye angry, and sin not

verse.note: The words reproduce the Septuagint of Psalm 4:4 (4:5 in its numbering). Most interpreters take the imperative not as a command to be angry but as a concession: when you are angry, do not let it lead to sin. Verse 31 goes on to say that anger is to be removed altogether.

verse.text: and do not give room to the devil.
Whoever steals must steal no longer, but must rather labor, doing what is good with their own hands, so as to have something to share with anyone in need.
Let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up where there is need, so that it may give grace to those who hear.
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be removed from you, along with all malice.
Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving each other just as God in Christ also forgave you.
So be imitators of God, as dearly loved children,
and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma.
But sexual immorality and impurity of any kind, or greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for holy ones,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'saints', which many translations keep; others use 'God's people'. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue, which is not the meaning here.

verse.text: nor obscenity, nor foolish talk or crude joking, which are out of place, but rather thanksgiving.
For of this you can be sure: no sexually immoral or impure or greedy person—that is, an idolater—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
So do not be partners with them;
for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the light is found in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
and discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
Take no part in the fruitless works of darkness, but rather expose them,
for it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret.
But everything that is exposed by the light becomes visible,
for everything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says: “Wake up, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
verse.note: The formula is the one used to introduce Scripture in 4:8, but the lines that follow do not match any known Old Testament passage, though they echo Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1. Most scholars think they come from an early Christian hymn, perhaps one sung at baptism. The source is not certain.

verse.text: So look carefully at how you walk, not as unwise people but as wise,
making the most of the time, because the days are evil.

note.term: making the most of the time

verse.note: The verb is a marketplace word meaning to buy up or buy back, and the noun for 'time' means a season or opportunity, not clock time. Most scholars take the phrase to mean seizing every opportunity while it lasts. The older rendering 'redeeming the time' keeps the commercial image but is now hard to understand.

verse.text: For this reason do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
And do not get drunk on wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled by the Spirit,
verse.note: The Greek preposition here normally marks means or sphere rather than content, so 'by the Spirit' is the more natural reading: the Spirit is the one who fills. Most English versions have 'with the Spirit', making the Spirit what one is filled with, and that reading remains possible. A minority read 'in spirit', referring to the human spirit.

verse.text: speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making music with your heart to the Lord,
giving thanks always for everything, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God the Father,
submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for 'fear', which also covers the awe and respect owed to someone of higher standing. The related verb is rendered 'show reverence for' in verse 33, so that the reader can see the section opens and closes with the same idea. Some translations keep 'fear' in both places; 'respect' is the common choice in verse 33.

verse.text: Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord,
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts, including Papyrus 46 and Codex Vaticanus, have no verb in this verse; it reads 'wives, to your own husbands as to the Lord', borrowing its verb from 'submitting to one another' in verse 21. Many other manuscripts supply the verb. English needs one, so it is supplied here, but the instruction to wives grammatically depends on the mutual submission of verse 21.

verse.text: for a husband is head of his wife as Christ also is head of the assembly, he himself being the savior of the body.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The metaphorical force of 'head' is disputed. Most lexicographers take it to mean one who holds authority or pre-eminence, a use found in the Septuagint for leaders; some scholars argue for 'source', as of a river. The literal word is kept because the passage plays on head and body.

verse.text: But as the assembly submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
so that he might make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word,

note.term: by the washing of water with the word
note.traditional: with the washing of water by the word

verse.note: The 'washing' is commonly taken as baptism, perhaps with the image of a bride's bath before her wedding in view. 'The word' is a term for something spoken; it may mean the proclaimed gospel, a confession made at baptism, or words spoken over the person baptised. The Greek does not settle which.

verse.text: so that he himself might present the assembly to himself in glory, having no stain or wrinkle or anything of the sort, but so that she might be holy and without blemish.
In the same way husbands too ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. The one who loves his own wife loves himself,
for no one ever hated his own flesh; rather, he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the assembly,
because we are members of his body.

note.traditional: members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'of his flesh and of his bones', echoing Genesis 2:23, and the King James Version includes the words. The earliest witnesses lack them, and most editors judge them a later expansion, though some argue they were dropped by accident.

text.q: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”

verse.text: This mystery is great, but I am speaking of Christ and the assembly.
verse.note: In Paul's usage the word means a secret in God's purposes, once hidden and now disclosed, not a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Here the secret is that the 'one flesh' union of Genesis 2:24 points to Christ and the assembly. The Latin Vulgate rendered the word sacramentum, which shaped the later view of marriage as a sacrament.

verse.text: In any case, each one of you as well must love his own wife as himself, and the wife is to show reverence for her husband.
Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verse.note: This translation normally renders this adjective as “righteous” or “just”, but here it describes a course of action, not a person, and plain English says “this is right”, as most versions do. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (right/righteous/righteousness and just/justice), so the same root lies behind “the breastplate of righteousness” in verse 14.

verse.text: “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise,

text.q: “so that it may go well with you and you may live long on the earth.”

verse.note: The quotation is the commandment of Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16 in its Greek form. There the promise concerns long life in “the land that the Lord your God is giving you”, and the Greek word can mean either “land” or “earth”. The letter leaves out the clause about the land God is giving, which makes the promise read as a general one.

verse.text: And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in sincerity of heart, as you would Christ,
not serving only when watched, as people-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ doing the will of God, wholeheartedly

note.traditional: doing the will of God from the heart

verse.note: The Greek phrase, literally “from the soul”, sits between two clauses and can attach to either. Most English versions join it to what precedes (“doing the will of God from the heart”). The punctuation of the Greek edition translated here joins it to what follows (“wholeheartedly serving with goodwill”), and the translation follows that.

verse.text: serving with goodwill, as for the Lord and not for people,
knowing that whatever good each person does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether slave or free.
And masters, do the same to them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in the heavens, and there is no favoritism with him.

note.traditional: your Master / their Lord and yours

verse.note: Greek uses one word, kyrios, for both a slave’s “master” and “the Lord”. Throughout verses 5–9 the passage plays on this: slaves serve earthly masters as serving the Lord, and masters are reminded that they have a Master of their own. English has to choose between “master” and “Lord” each time, which hides the repetition.

The Greek is plural, a turn of phrase carried over from Hebrew and from the Greek Old Testament. Most English translations flatten it to “heaven”. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it.

verse.text: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.
Put on the full armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil,

because our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that you may be able to withstand on the evil day and, having done everything, to stand.
verse.note: The verb can mean “accomplish, carry through” or “overcome, subdue”. Most translations take it as having made every preparation or done all that the fight requires. On the other reading it means “having defeated all opponents”. Either fits the military picture.

verse.text: Stand, then, with truth belted around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness on,
and with your feet shod in the readiness of the good news of peace,
verse.note: The Greek leaves open how “readiness” relates to “the good news of peace”. It may be the readiness or firm footing that the good news gives, or a readiness to go and announce it. The rendering keeps the Greek’s open phrasing; commentators are divided.

“Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news”.

verse.text: in every situation taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to put out all the flaming arrows of the evil one.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
through every prayer and petition, praying on every occasion in the Spirit, and to that end keeping watch with all perseverance and petition for all the holy ones,
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people”.

verse.text: and for me, that a word may be given to me when I open my mouth, to make known boldly the secret of the good news,
verse.note: The traditional “mystery” suggests to a modern reader something puzzling or beyond understanding. In the usage of the period, including the Greek book of Daniel, the word means a secret, here one that God kept hidden and has now disclosed, which is why it can be “made known”. Most English versions keep “mystery”, and scholars generally explain it in this sense.

verse.text: for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that in declaring it I may speak boldly, as I must.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary term for serving as an official envoy. Envoys were by long custom treated as inviolable, so an ambassador in chains is a deliberate paradox. The Greek word for “chain” is singular.

verse.text: So that you also may know how things are with me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make everything known to you.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts.
Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address or refer to a mixed group of men and women as members of one family, and here it means the whole community. Older versions have “brethren” or “brothers”; several modern translations render it as here. In verse 21 the singular refers to one man and is translated “brother”.

verse.text: Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with undying love.
verse.note: The letter’s last words are literally “in imperishability”, and what they modify is disputed. They may describe the love of those who love Christ, as translated here and in most versions. They may instead go with “grace” (“grace and immortality be with all…”), or describe Christ as the one who lives in immortality.
